what_it_is: EngVQA is a multimodal benchmark of 696 diagram-dependent problems in five engineering subjects (dynamics 171, thermodynamics 236, fluid mechanics 93, heat and mass transfer 96, mechanics of materials 100), extracted semi-automatically from question PDFs and manually checked against the reference material (p.1, p.3, p.6). Its evaluator, EngJudge, has the model write its solution in eight tagged stages (problem characterization, assumptions, visual interpretation, equation selection, logical reasoning, algebraic accuracy, physical interpretation, final answer); an LLM judge scores each stage against the reference solution images by penalty deductions and fatal-error caps, propagates scores along a stage dependency graph, and applies LLM checks of verbosity, coverage and physical sanity to give a 0-10 score (p.4-6, p.18-19, p.31). Two generators are evaluated, Qwen3-VL-8B and Gemini-2.5-Flash, with Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview as the main evaluator and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct as a second (p.6). The human check had nine students rate the judge's scores on four problems each (p.8, p.23).
domain: engineering: dynamics, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, heat and mass transfer, mechanics of materials, with technical diagrams; vision-language models (p.1, p.3)
size: 696 problems (p.1, p.3); 2 generator models, 2 evaluator models (p.6)
source_of_items: existing problems with worked solutions ('standard academic engineering physics problems', p.9), extracted from question PDFs with Adobe PDF Extract, PyMuPDF and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite and manually verified (p.6); the source books are not named, though problem labels such as 'Thermodynamics, Problem 5-131' suggest textbook exercises (p.17, p.22)
has_gold_traces: partial: each problem has a reference worked solution, given to the judge as images (p.31); no machine-checkable intermediate values
evaluation: step-level or process, by LLM judge: each of eight stages scored by a stage-specific LLM-judge prompt against the reference, starting at 10 with penalties of 2, 4, 7 or 10 and caps for fatal errors (p.5, p.18); the final answer is judged by relative error (within 5% no penalty, 5-10% moderate, above 10% major), applied by the judge (p.5); dependency propagation and three solution-level LLM meta-checks (p.6, p.19); 11 judge calls per solution (p.9)
human_validation: Nine undergraduate/graduate students (p.8), four randomly assigned problems each, rating Gemini-2.5-Flash solutions (p.8, p.23). They first marked each stage correct or incorrect without seeing EngJudge's evaluation, but no agreement figure for these labels is reported (p.22-23). They then saw EngJudge's score and rated it on a five-point scale from 'much too low' to 'much too high'; a 'human score' was reconstructed as EngJudge's score plus an adjustment of -2 to +2 (p.23). The headline Pearson 0.975 and MAE 0.67 are between EngJudge's score and that reconstructed score, over 393 data points (285 stage ratings, 108 meta-check ratings) (p.8, p.23); 48.9% of ratings were 'About right' (p.25). The extracted items were also manually verified (p.6).
contamination_measures: none; the limitations say contamination cannot be fully ruled out (p.9)

engtrace_use.explanation: Belongs in: the engineering paragraph; its validation figures also bear on the judge-validity paragraph. Candidate, not cited in the May paper. It contradicts two May claims if carried over: 'no existing benchmark verifies this process' (May p.1) and 'existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching' (May p.3), since EngVQA scores eight solution stages (p.5). Its headline human agreement (Pearson 0.975, p.1, p.8) is not agreement with independent human grades (p.23), which matters if the revision compares validation evidence.

suggested_wording: EngVQA (Wasiq et al., 2026) has an LLM judge score eight solution stages of vision-language models against reference solutions on 696 diagram-based problems from five engineering subjects; its human check had nine students rate the judge's scores on four problems each.

overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: engineering subjects that overlap EngTrace's mechanical and chemical branches (fluid mechanics, mechanics of materials, thermodynamics, heat transfer); evaluation of the solution process beyond the final answer; a human check of the evaluator. Lacks: generated instances (696 static extracted problems, p.6); gold intermediate values computed by code (references are solution images read by the judge, p.31); any deterministic step check (every stage is judged by an LLM, p.5); evaluator validation independent of the judge's own score (p.23); model breadth (two generators, p.6). Different scope: vision-language models on diagrams. What EngTrace adds: text-only instances generated from templates in five branches; gold values computed by the template code and checked deterministically (answer, milestones, per-claim arithmetic), with an LLM judge only for milestones those checks miss; and an evaluator validated against step and milestone labels from 15 experts (X1: 300 traces, three own-branch experts per trace).
notes: (1) The Pearson 0.975 is between EngJudge's score and a 'human score' defined as that same score shifted by at most 2 points from a rating given after seeing it (p.23). With scores spread over 0-10 a high correlation follows largely by construction, and the independent correct/incorrect stage labels collected first are not reported (p.22-23). The search note's 'Pearson 0.975 against 9 students' grades' should not be repeated as agreement with human grading. (2) Scores depend heavily on the evaluator: EngJudge gives Gemini-2.5-Flash 2.869 under Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview and 0.945 under Qwen3-VL-32B (p.20). (3) The abstract benchmarks 'multiple state-of-the-art open and closed source VLMs' (p.1); the experiments use two (p.6). (4) Internal inconsistencies: the preference for dependency scoring is 66.7% in the text (p.8-9, p.25) and 63.6% in Figure 13 (p.25); the raters are 'undergraduate/graduate students' (p.8), 'expert participants' (p.23) and 'volunteer graduate engineering students' (p.9). (5) No dataset or code link appears in the text.
